q: Your competitive programming input limit is n ≤ 500. Which DP family and time complexity normally fits without timing out?
o: Interval DP in O(n³) time
500³ ≈ 1.25 × 10⁸ operations, the classic sweet spot for Interval DP like Matrix Chain or Optimal BST.
Subset Bitmask DP in O(2ⁿ n²)
2⁵⁰⁰ is astronomically too large; Subset DP needs n ≤ 20.
Exponential recursion in O(2ⁿ)
Without memoization, overlapping subproblems blow up past n ≈ 40.
O(n²) is required because O(n³) always times out
For n ≤ 500, tight O(n³) loops run well inside a 1-second limit.
e: Size limits map straight to paradigms: n ≤ 20 fits O(2ⁿ n²), n ≤ 500 fits O(n³) Interval DP, n ≤ 5,000 fits O(n²), and n ≤ 10⁶ needs O(n log n) or O(V+E).

q: Why does caching (memoizing) fib(n) collapse an O(2ⁿ) recursion tree into an O(n) DAG?
o: Because there are only n+1 distinct subproblems, and each is computed once and reused via shared pointers
Repeated calls to fib(k) point to the same cached node instead of spawning a fresh subtree.
Because memoization deletes the base cases fib(0) and fib(1)
Base cases are still needed to stop recursion.
Because it changes the recurrence formula from addition to multiplication
The recurrence stays identical; only duplicate work is eliminated.
Because a DAG allows cycles back to fib(n)
Dependencies remain strictly acyclic from larger n down to smaller subproblems.
e: Overlapping subproblems turn an exponential tree into a linear-size DAG of unique states.

q: In Longest Common Subsequence (LCS), when characters X[i] and Y[j] match, which arrow direction points back to the subproblem used?
o: Diagonal ↖ to c[i−1, j−1] plus 1
Matching characters are consumed from both strings, adding 1 to the top-left diagonal value.
Up ↑ to c[i−1, j] plus 1
Up ↑ skips X[i] when characters do not match.
Left ← to c[i, j−1] plus 1
Left ← skips Y[j] when characters do not match.
Right → to c[i, j+1]
DP fills forward; arrows always point backward to smaller indices.
e: A match X[i] = Y[j] extends c[i−1, j−1] by 1 (↖). Mismatches take max(c[i−1, j] ↑, c[i, j−1] ←).

q: What does parent[i] store in the O(n²) Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) algorithm?
o: The index of the previous element j < i that gave the longest chain ending at i
Following parent[i] backward reconstructs the actual sequence, not just its length.
The total number of elements smaller than A[i]
Counting smaller items does not guarantee an increasing chain.
The maximum element anywhere in A[0..n−1]
parent[i] links specifically to the predecessor in the subsequence ending at i.
The subarray sum up to index i
Subarray sum belongs to Kadane's algorithm, not LIS.
e: Whenever dp[j] + 1 > dp[i] with A[j] < A[i], we update both dp[i] and parent[i] = j.

q: When compressing 0/1 Knapsack to a 1D rolling array dp[0..W], why must capacity c loop backward from W down to wᵢ?
o: So dp[c − wᵢ] still holds the previous row's value (without item i), preventing item i from being used multiple times
Looping forward overwrites dp[c − wᵢ] first, turning 0/1 Knapsack into Unbounded Knapsack.
Because backward loops run faster in CPU caches than forward loops
The reason is correctness (avoiding item reuse), not cache speed.
So the base case dp[0] gets overwritten at the end
dp[0] stays 0 because c stops at wᵢ ≥ 1.
Because weights wᵢ can be negative in 0/1 Knapsack
Standard 0/1 Knapsack assumes positive integer weights.
e: Right-to-left (c = W down to wᵢ) ensures dp[c − wᵢ] comes from row i − 1, preserving the 0/1 single-use rule.

q: Why must Matrix Chain Multiplication fill table m[i, j] along diagonals of increasing length l = 2 … n instead of row-by-row top-to-bottom?
o: Because m[i, j] depends on shorter sub-chains m[i, k] (left) and m[k+1, j] (below), so row i needs row k+1 already filled
Every split (i..k) and (k+1..j) has strictly smaller length than (i..j).
Because matrix dimensions pᵢ are only known along the main diagonal
All dimensions p₀..pₙ are known upfront.
Because lower-triangular cells i > j store the inverse matrices
Cells with i > j are unused because an interval requires i ≤ j.
Because diagonal fill reduces time complexity from O(n³) to O(n²)
Time remains O(n³); diagonal order is required for dependency correctness.
e: Increasing interval length l = j − i + 1 guarantees both m[i, k] and m[k+1, j] are already solved.

q: In Optimal Binary Search Tree (OBST), why is w[i, j] added to the recurrence e[i, j] = min(e[i, r−1] + e[r+1, j]) + w[i, j]?
o: Picking root r pushes every key and dummy node in [i, j] one level deeper, increasing every search cost by 1 × its probability
Their total probability weight is exactly w[i, j].
w[i, j] counts how many times root r is rotated during AVL balancing
OBST is static; there are no rotations.
w[i, j] subtracts the dummy key probabilities from the root
Dummy keys are included inside w[i, j] because unsuccessful searches also deepen by 1.
w[i, j] is only added when r = i
All nodes in the subtree—left, right, and root—gain +1 depth relative to the subtree root.
e: Increasing subtree depth by 1 adds the sum of all subtree probabilities w[i, j] once.

q: In Held-Karp exact TSP DP dp[S, v], in what order are states filled?
o: By increasing subset size |S| = 2, 3, …, n
dp[S, v] reads dp[S \ {v}, u], whose subset size is strictly |S| − 1.
By decreasing vertex index v = n−1 down to 0
Order of v within the same |S| doesn't matter, but smaller subsets |S|−1 must finish first.
By sorting edges in decreasing weight order
Held-Karp enumerates subsets and endpoints, not greedy edges.
Only along the main diagonal S = {v}
|S|=1 is just the base case; we need all subsets up to size n.
e: Increasing |S| guarantees S \ {v} is already computed when evaluating dp[S, v].

q: During DFS on a directed graph, edge (u, v) is explored and vertex v is currently GRAY (discovered, not yet finished). What kind of edge is (u, v)?
o: A Back edge, which proves the graph contains a directed cycle
A gray vertex is an active ancestor on the recursion stack, so pointing to it closes a cycle.
A Forward edge to a finished descendant
Forward edges point to BLACK descendants.
A Cross edge between finished subtrees
Cross edges point to BLACK non-ancestors.
A Tree edge discovering a new vertex
Tree edges always land on WHITE vertices.
e: DFS target color gives the edge class immediately: WHITE → Tree, GRAY → Back (cycle!), BLACK → Forward (if d[u] < d[v]) or Cross (if d[u] > d[v]).

q: What does Kahn's algorithm push into its queue to build a topological ordering?
o: Every vertex whose remaining in-degree reaches 0
Zero in-degree means all prerequisites are finished, so it is safe to output next.
Every vertex with the highest out-degree
Out-degree does not ensure prerequisites are done.
Every vertex discovered by a back edge
Topological sort only exists for DAGs (no back edges).
Vertices sorted alphabetically
Order must respect directed dependencies.
e: Kahn's queue tracks in-degree-0 vertices and decrements neighbors' in-degrees as each vertex is popped.

q: Why can Dijkstra's algorithm give the wrong shortest path when a graph has negative edge weights (even with no negative cycles)?
o: Dijkstra locks a popped vertex's distance permanently; a later negative edge from another path can never revise it
Once popped from the min-PQ, Dijkstra assumes no future path can be shorter.
Dijkstra requires the graph to be a tree
Dijkstra works on general directed/undirected graphs with non-negative weights.
Priority queues cannot store negative numbers
Min-heaps store negatives fine; the greedy finality assumption breaks.
Dijkstra only relaxes each edge once in alphabetical order
Dijkstra relaxes outgoing edges in greedy distance order.
e: Use Bellman-Ford (O(VE)) when negative weights exist, or DAG-SP (O(V+E)) on acyclic graphs.

q: How does Bellman-Ford detect a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source?
o: Run one extra (|V|-th) pass over all edges; if any edge (u, v) still relaxes d[v] > d[u] + w(u,v), a negative cycle exists
Shortest simple paths have at most |V|−1 edges, so relaxing on pass |V| proves a negative cycle.
Check if any single edge weight w(u,v) is less than 0
A negative edge without a negative cycle still has well-defined shortest paths.
Check if the graph has any forward edges in DFS
Forward edges do not create cycles.
Run Dijkstra twice from the sink
Dijkstra fails on negative edges.
e: After |V|−1 passes, all simple paths are settled. Any further improvement on pass |V| means a negative cycle.

q: What does AC-3 (Arc Consistency) do before or during Sudoku backtracking?
o: Shrinks candidate domains by removing values in cell X that have no valid match in constrained neighbor Y
Domain propagation prunes dead ends early before branching deeply.
Replaces backtracking with Dijkstra's shortest path
AC-3 shrinks domains; search still branches if multiple candidates remain.
Guesses random digits in all empty cells simultaneously
AC-3 is deterministic constraint propagation.
Sorts the grid rows by sum
Sudoku constrains distinct digits in rows, columns, and boxes.
e: AC-3 enforces pairwise consistency, shrinking domains like {1,2,3,4} down to a single forced digit.

q: In 0/1 Knapsack Branch-and-Bound, when can a subtree at node u be safely pruned?
o: Whenever its fractional upper bound ub ≤ best_so_far (or W_rem < 0)
Even allowing fractional parts of remaining items cannot beat the integer solution already found.
Whenever its current integer profit v_so_far < best_so_far
Remaining capacity might still push total profit above best_so_far.
Whenever an item is excluded (right child)
Skipping a heavy item often unlocks higher-profit combinations.
Only after reaching a leaf node
Branch-and-bound's power comes from pruning internal subtrees early.
e: The fractional relaxation gives a valid upper bound; if ub ≤ best_so_far, no integer completion can improve the best answer.

q: Which pair correctly contrasts a polynomial-time (P) problem with a deceptively similar NP-hard counterpart?
o: Eulerian Cycle (P) vs. Hamiltonian Cycle (NPC)
Visiting every edge once is O(E) via even degrees; visiting every vertex once is NP-complete.
Shortest Path (NPC) vs. Longest Simple Path (P)
It is the opposite: Shortest Path is in P, while Longest Simple Path is NP-hard.
3-Coloring (P) vs. 2-Coloring (NPC)
2-Coloring is O(V+E) bipartite BFS; 3-Coloring is NP-complete.
0/1 Knapsack (P) vs. Fractional Knapsack (NPC)
Fractional Knapsack is greedy O(n log n); 0/1 Knapsack is NP-hard.
e: Know the boundary: Shortest Path, 2-Coloring, Eulerian Cycle, and Fractional Knapsack are in P; Longest Path, 3-Coloring, Hamiltonian Cycle, and 0/1 Knapsack are NP-hard.

q: To prove a new language B is NP-hard using a known NP-complete problem A, which reduction direction is required?
o: Reduce A ≤ₚ B: map every instance x of known hard A into an instance F(x) of B in polynomial time
If a fast decider existed for B, F plus that decider would solve known hard A fast too.
Reduce B ≤ₚ A: map instances of B into A
Reducing B to A only proves B is no harder than A, which says nothing about hardness!
Prove B has a polynomial-time decider
That would put B in P, not prove NP-hardness.
Show x ∈ A implies F(x) ∈ B without checking the reverse direction
Both directions (x ∈ A ⇔ F(x) ∈ B) are mandatory.
e: Always reduce KNOWN HARD (A) ≤ₚ TARGET (B) and prove both correctness directions.

q: In the 3-SAT ≤ₚ Independent Set gadget with k clauses, why do we add conflict edges between xᵢ and ¬xᵢ across triangles?
o: To forbid picking both xᵢ = True and xᵢ = False simultaneously in an independent set of size k
An edge between xᵢ and ¬xᵢ ensures at most one of the two truth values can be chosen.
To make every clause triangle into a 4-clique
Clause edges already form a 3-clique (triangle); conflict edges enforce variable consistency.
To ensure the graph is bipartite
Clause triangles are odd cycles of length 3, so the graph is not bipartite.
To reduce the number of vertices from 3k to k
The graph keeps all 3k literal vertices; k is the target independent set size.
e: Triangle edges allow ≤ 1 vertex per clause; conflict edges force consistent variable truth values across clauses.

q: What property must edge weights satisfy for APPROX-TSP-TOUR (MST + preorder shortcutting) to guarantee a 2-approximation?
o: The triangle inequality: c(u, w) ≤ c(u, v) + c(v, w)
Shortcutting skipped vertices only avoids increasing tour cost when direct edges are no longer than detours.
All edge weights must be negative
Metric TSP weights are non-negative.
The graph must be a DAG
TSP tours run on complete undirected graphs.
All edge weights must be distinct powers of 2
Weights only need to obey metric symmetry and the triangle inequality.
e: Without the triangle inequality, General TSP is inapproximable within any constant factor unless P = NP.

q: In the Subset-Sum FPTAS, why does TRIM(L, δ) set δ = ε / (2n)?
o: Because n trimming steps compound multiplicatively as (1 + ε/(2n))ⁿ ≤ e^(ε/2) ≤ 1 + ε
Dividing by 2n keeps accumulated relative error across n items strictly below ε.
Because δ must equal 2n so every element is trimmed
Setting δ = 2n would delete almost the entire list.
Because target sum t is always equal to 2n
n is the item count, independent of target t.
To make the algorithm run in O(2ⁿ) exponential time
Trimming keeps list sizes polynomial in n and 1/ε.
e: Using δ = ε/(2n) bounds total compounded multiplicative error by (1+δ)ⁿ ≤ 1 + ε while keeping lists polynomial.

q: Is 0/1 Knapsack's O(nW) DP algorithm a true polynomial-time algorithm?
o: No — it is pseudo-polynomial, because W is exponential in the bit length (log₂ W) of the input capacity
Doubling the bits of W squares W itself, blowing up O(nW).
Yes — because n and W are multiplied once
Complexity is measured in input bit-size, not numeric value W.
Yes — as long as W ≤ 10⁶
Asymptotic polynomiality applies to arbitrary input sizes, not fixed caps.
No — because it runs in O(n³) time
O(n³) would actually be polynomial; O(nW) depends on numeric value W.
e: O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial; to get a true FPTAS in O(n³/ε), scale item values by K = ε·v_max / n.
